title: Third-party hearing rights: public-interest intervention and mutually exclusive applications
shortTitle: Third-party hearing rights: public-interest intervention and mutually exclusive applications
summary: A third party may sometimes demand participation because it represents interests the agency must hear or because granting another application effectively decides its own.
notes:
Third parties ordinarily cannot demand a hearing solely to adjudicate someone else’s rights. The assigned notes identify two important statutory settings. In Office of Communication of the United Church of Christ v. FCC, a local church and civil-rights activists alleged that a Mississippi station refused programming supporting desegregation. Their participation could inform the FCC’s required public-interest finding on renewal, and the court required an opportunity to present those concerns in the hearing process.

Ashbacker involved two broadcast applications that could not both be granted under a geographic-frequency rule. The FCC summarily granted Fetzer’s application and then treated that grant as a conclusive obstacle at Ashbacker’s hearing. The Supreme Court required a comparative hearing because otherwise Ashbacker’s statutory right to a hearing before denial would be empty. The editors emphasize that Ashbacker did not specify every hearing detail and that later statutes and practices use auctions for many commercial licenses. Mere competitive disadvantage, as in the cited pipeline and tower cases, does not establish the mutual exclusivity necessary for that rationale.
